hints.junior: SameSite=Lax blocks cross-site POSTs — it does not block a cross-site GET, and GET links show up in admin panels more than you'd expect.
hints.mid: "We set SameSite, CSRF is handled" treats a scoped browser rule as a blanket fix — any endpoint outside that scope, most often a GET route, isn't protected at all.
hints.staff: SameSite's 'same site' is the registrable domain, not the origin — an attacker-influenced subdomain of your own domain is still 'same-site' to the cookie.

hints.junior: Click 'Simulate cross-site attack' in each mode and watch whether the simulated attacker page manages to trigger the state change.
hints.mid: The vulnerable version fires over a plain GET link and the cookie rides along; the hardened version blocks both the GET-based mutation and the cross-site POST attempt.
hints.staff: The hardened log shows two independent rejections — the SameSite cookie policy blocks the cross-site POST on its own, and the missing CSRF token would've blocked it too, that overlap is the defense-in-depth point.

hints.junior: Strict never sends the cookie cross-site at all, even for a clicked link. Lax sends it for a top-level GET navigation but blocks it on cross-site POSTs, image loads, and fetch calls.
hints.mid: A hidden auto-submitting cross-site POST form or an img tag pointed at your endpoint doesn't get the Lax cookie attached — that's exactly the shape Lax was built to block. A clicked link or JS-driven top-level redirect does.
hints.staff: SameSite closes the gap only for requests shaped the way it was designed to gate — it does nothing to fix an app that exposes state changes over GET, that's a separate, older mistake SameSite can't retroactively patch.

hints.junior: Never implement a delete/revoke/transfer action behind a plain GET link — that rule predates SameSite and is exactly why the Lax carve-out for top-level GET still matters.
hints.mid: uploads.victim.com and app.victim.com are the same registrable domain, so a cookie scoped there treats both as same-site even if one is a lower-trust subdomain an attacker can influence.
hints.staff: SameSite is enforced client-side only — non-browser HTTP clients and some WebViews don't implement it correctly, and the server has no way to verify a client honored it. Server-side token validation is the only half the server can actually check.

sections.junior: Today's case is about SameSite cookies and CSRF — specifically the gap that survives even after you've set SameSite equals Lax correctly, because Lax was never designed to block a plain cross-site GET request.

Strict blocks the cookie on every cross-site request, even a clicked link. Lax blocks cross-site posts and subresource loads, but still allows the cookie through on a top-level GET navigation, which is exactly the gap that matters here.
Try simulating a cross-site attack against each version of the endpoint and watch whether the action actually fires.
Never put a state-changing action behind a GET request. SameSite is scoped protection, not a blanket fix, and a real CSRF token is still the check the server can actually verify.
